name: EliStore
subtitle: Apps that never made it to the App Store.
description: EliStore is a private source for AltStore and SideStore. It hosts apps built for hardware Apple never cared about and services that lost their official client — installed straight onto the phone, no App Store review in the way.

apps.name: DS get
apps.subtitle: The Download Station remote Synology retired.
apps.localizedDescription:
A rebuild of Synology's DS get — the Download Station remote that was pulled from the app stores — written against Synology's official Download Station Web API. It talks to your own NAS directly. No Synology account, no vendor cloud, no third party in the middle.

Everything the original did, mapped one-to-one onto the documented API:

• Task list with live progress, size, per-task down/up speed, ETA and destination folder. Six filter tabs and six sort orders.
• Task detail with the original's five tabs — General, Transfer, Files, Trackers, Peers. The BT-only tabs hide themselves for HTTP, FTP and NZB downloads.
• Add downloads from HTTP/FTP URLs, magnet links and ED2K links (several at once), or by opening a .torrent or .nzb file from anywhere in iOS. Optional site credentials, unzip password and destination folder.
• Pause, resume, delete with “keep partial files”, change destination, resume-all, pause-all, clear-completed.
• Multi-select — long-press a task to start selecting, then act on the batch.
• BT Search across the search modules enabled in Download Station, with server-side sorting and category filtering.
• RSS feeds configured on the NAS, their items, manual refresh and download from an item.
• Settings for speed limits, download schedule, eMule service, auto-extract and default destination.
• Several NASes, switchable, each with its own saved session, reachable by address or by QuickConnect ID from anywhere — LAN, DDNS, SmartDNS or Synology's relay, whichever answers.
• A share extension: send a magnet or a link into DS get from any app.
• A destination browser over File Station, with a typed-path fallback.
• 2-step verification, including “trust this device”.
• Global transfer rates in the header.

Session IDs and 2-step device tokens live in the Keychain. Passwords are never written to disk, and every login is sent as a POST body so credentials never appear in a URL or a log. A per-server “accept self-signed certificate” switch trusts your NAS's certificate for that host only, leaving normal validation in place everywhere else.

Requires Download Station on a Synology NAS running DSM 6 or 7.

privacy.name: LocalNetwork
privacy.usageDescription: DS get connects to your Synology NAS on your local network to manage Download Station.

versions.localizedDescription:
You stay signed in now, and the login screen is rebuilt to match the original app.

Sessions expire on the NAS's own schedule, and the app treated that as a dead end — it cleared everything and returned to a login screen that remembered nothing, so getting back in meant re-entering the QuickConnect ID, the account and the password even without leaving the house. "Remember me" now keeps the password in the Keychain, pinned to this device and readable only while it is unlocked, and an expired session triggers a silent sign-in instead of a logout. Signing out deliberately still forgets the password; an expired session does not.

The login screen is one field taking either an address or a QuickConnect ID, then account and password, with HTTPS and "Remember me" inline — and it accepts host:port for a NAS on a non-standard port. Editing a NAS and typing on the login screen now stay in step in both directions.

Also fixed: ports are validated against 1–65535 rather than silently saving something like 59998080, and "Remember me" no longer switches itself off between tapping it and signing in.

Uploading a .torrent works now. 1.2 fixed adding downloads by URL; this fixes the file-upload path, which was failing the same way for a different reason.

1.2 deliberately left uploads on the classic API, on the grounds that the newer one pairs the upload with an array of filename hash codes and looked fragile to reproduce for no gain. That was the wrong call — it was exactly the failing path. The real contract names each uploaded part by an Apache HashCodeBuilder hash of its filename, sends every parameter as its own form-data part, and quotes "file" as a JSON string where the URL case wants a bare word. Both the app and the web build now reproduce all of it, falling back to the classic upload only where the NAS does not advertise SYNO.DownloadStation2.Task.

Adding a download works. It never did before — this fixes 1.0 and 1.1 alike.

Creating a task always failed with error 101. The cause was the API version, not the destination: DSM 7 advertises SYNO.DownloadStation.Task maxVersion 3, this client negotiated the highest available, and create at v3 rejects the documented uri parameter. Error 101 is a generic "invalid parameter" and says nothing about the version, which is what made it look like a destination problem.

Both the app and the web build now send the same versions Synology's own client does: v1 for list, getinfo, pause, resume and delete; v2 for edit; and SYNO.DownloadStation2.Task v1 for create where the NAS advertises it, falling back to the classic API at v2. File uploads stay on the classic API, which is what the published spec documents.

QuickConnect now works from outside your own network.

Resolution was broken three ways at once: only the first step ran, so the relay address was never fetched; every candidate was built as https, which can never reach a NAS publishing plain HTTP on 5000; and the relay was assumed to speak TLS when it speaks HTTP. Candidates are now tried LAN first and relay last, and each one is checked against the NAS's own ezid so it cannot connect to a stranger's DiskStation at the same private address on a foreign network. The QuickConnect ID is stored with the server and re-resolved whenever the address stops answering.

New: a share extension — share a magnet or a link from any app straight into DS get. New: a real destination browser over File Station, instead of only top-level shared folders.

Also fixed: leaving the destination on the default now sends Download Station's own default explicitly, .torrent and .nzb files actually associate with the app, and an ATS key was removed whose mere presence made iOS block the public relay hostname.

apps.name: StormDrive
apps.subtitle: Drive Anki Overdrive cars, no servers required.
apps.localizedDescription:
A native iPhone app for driving Anki Overdrive and Anki Drive cars, talking the vehicle protocol directly over Bluetooth LE. No Anki servers, no accounts — the cars work exactly as they always did.

GARAGE
Finds every car in range, shows signal and battery, one tap to connect. Multiple cars at once.

DRIVE
Four interchangeable control schemes — throttle + lane pads, tilt steering, virtual joystick, or an MFi / PlayStation / Xbox controller. Live speed dial, lane position, battery and a speed trace. Boost, U-turn, headlights and a hard stop. The lightning storm behind the HUD answers to how fast the car is actually going.

RACE
Countdown, lap timing, live leaderboard with best and last laps, and a session-record highlight. Autopilot can drive a car for you at three aggression levels.

TRACK
Drive one slow lap and the app maps the layout, then draws it as a live map with every car moving on it.

SETUP
Control scheme, speed ceilings, storm intensity, haptics, and a demo mode that runs three simulated cars so you can try everything with no hardware in range.

Works with the original Anki Drive and Anki Overdrive vehicles. Bluetooth permission is required; tilt steering additionally asks for motion access the first time you pick it.

privacy.name: Bluetooth
privacy.usageDescription: StormDrive uses Bluetooth to find and drive your Anki Overdrive cars.

privacy.name: Motion
privacy.usageDescription: Tilt steering uses the motion sensors to steer your car.

apps.name: Expenses
apps.subtitle: Mileage, receipts and travel, straight into Excel.
apps.localizedDescription:
Expense tracking for two companies at once — mileage, running costs, meetings and travel — with the Excel file accounting actually wants at the end of it.

MILEAGE
Pick a starting point and a destination anywhere in Slovenia or Croatia — a town, or a specific address — with stops on the way if the day had them. The distance is looked up along real roads and multiplied by the rate, doubled for a return journey. Every figure stays editable — a calculated distance is a suggestion, not a verdict.

DRIVE RECORDER
Say you are driving before you pull away and the phone counts the kilometres as you go, including while it is locked in your pocket. Stop, and it names the towns you started and finished in and hands you a mileage claim with the distance already filled in.

RECEIPTS
Photograph one and the amount, date and supplier are read off it and entered for you. It happens on the device — no upload, no account, no waiting on a server. Slovenian, Croatian, German and English receipts all work; it knows that SKUPAJ and UKUPNO mean the total and that DDV does not.

MEETINGS
Where it was, who you met, and the people present with their roles — the part that gets asked about later. As many guests and as many cost lines as the evening had.

TRAVEL
Any European or Balkan country, with flights, hotels, taxis, trains, meals and fair fees. A Belgrade hotel bill stays in dinars, with the euro figure worked out from a rate you can correct, so the claim still matches the receipt. Outside the EU roaming area it says so and offers the eSIM line before the phone bill reminds you.

SYNC
The iPhone and the Mac reconcile over your own Wi-Fi, with an encrypted link keyed to a six-digit code you type once. Nothing goes to anyone's server.

EXPORT
A workbook with a summary sheet and one sheet per kind of expense, cost lines broken out, real dates and euro formatting — plus CSV, and a backup file that carries the receipt photos with it.

Everything stays on the device until you export it.

privacy.usageDescription: Recording the kilometres of a drive, including while the app is in the background, and filling in where a journey started.

versions.localizedDescription:
Journeys can now start and end at an address, not just a town.

Type a street or a place name and it completes as you go, the way Maps does — "Dunajska cesta 50" finds the Ljubljana one and the Lukovica one and lets you say which. The distance is then measured to that door rather than to the middle of the town, which for a customer on the far edge of somewhere is a different claim. Addresses you have used before are offered first, since the same customers come round again, and "Where I am now" gives the street you are standing in.

Towns still work exactly as before and still work with no signal; addresses need a connection.

Also: the bottom row of an editor no longer scrolls underneath the total bar.

Sync between the iPhone and the Mac over your own Wi-Fi.

One device offers to sync and shows a six-digit code, the other finds it and enters it. The link is encrypted with a key derived from that code, so nothing readable crosses the network. The newest version of each entry wins, and a deletion on one device is a deletion on both rather than something the other device helpfully puts back.

Both devices need this version, and both need to be on the same network with the sync screen open on the one offering. iOS will ask for local network permission the first time.

• On the Mac, choosing a town opened a sheet with no room for the results — you could type into the search box but nothing could ever appear below it. The sheet now opens at a usable size with a proper search field.
• Five entries in the town list were not towns: GeoNames marks historical church seats with a code that the list builder mistook for an administrative seat, so searching "koper" offered the Roman Catholic Diocese of Koper alongside the town.

Fixes found while putting the store listing together.

• Opening a saved mileage claim looked the route up again and quietly replaced the distance — a claim you reopened to correct a typo could come back with a different amount. Saved claims are now left exactly as they were; Recalculate still does it on demand.
• A foreign-currency cost line lost precision as soon as you opened it: an exchange rate of 0,00854 was shown rounded to four places and then written back at that rounding, changing the total of a trip nobody had edited.
• The month picker on the Export screen came up blank instead of showing the current month.
• On the drive recorder the route name was squeezed to nothing and the Start button broke across two lines.
